newsitem.title: UK: POLL-Fine-tuning rates healthier for UK economy.
newsitem.headline: POLL-Fine-tuning rates healthier for UK economy.

text.p: Small and frequent adjustments to interest rates rather than fewer, larger changes were voted the best way to promote steady economic growth in Britain, a Reuters survey of economists showed on Thursday.
Twelve out of 23 respondents to the July 30 survey said they favoured a series of smaller changes in interest rates while seven said they preferred to see them moved in larger increments.
One said the scale of rises should depend on the economic environment, two said it made no difference to the economy and one gave no opinion.

Analysts said the "small but often" policy adopted by the Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee towards interest rate changes was in line with international practice and showed that Britain had joined the ranks of low-inflation countries.

"We are in a low inflation, low interest rate environment and the UK authorities are taking the view that quarter-point increments are the norm," said Ian Amstad, senior economist at Bankers Trust Company.
"They are following the normal practice on continental Europe of using monetary policy flexibly."

In the survey, 16 of the 23 economists said they expected a 25 basis point rise in base rates to seven percent after council meets next week. Seven expect rates to be left unchanged. The announcement on any change is due on August 7.
Respondents said the committee favoured gradual rate movements as any radical change to monetary policy would be seen by the markets as a panic response and may hit investor confidence.
"The markets have got used to the idea of tinkering. It's a reflection of policy working," said Jeremy Hawkins, chief economist at Bank of America.
Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International, said he preferred the gradual approach as there was a risk of overkill.

"By the time higher base rates feed through next year, the impact of windfall gains (from recent building society conversions) will have disappeared. The risk is that you do too much, too soon," he said.
With base rates at 6.75 percent and headline inflation at 2.9 percent year-on-year in June, real interest rates are currently running at around 3.75 percent.
Of the economists who favoured larger rises, most cited sterling's recent strength as the main reason.
Expectations of further interest rate rises have propelled the pound higher on foreign exchange markets, triggering concern among British exporters who say the trend is hitting overseas demand.

"The markets are aware that interest rate rises are inevitable and the small increases are keeping speculative pressure on the pound," said Deborah Barlow, economist at the Centre for Economic and Business Research. "Manufacturing is taking the brunt."
May manufacturing output fell 1.1 percent month-on-month after a rise of 0.5 percent in April.
Despite recent declines, sterling has remained robust in Europe, touching an eight-year high of 3.0878 marks on July 23.
David Hillier, chief UK economist at BZW said the shock of big rises would subdue consumer exuberance.
"The effect would be seen immediately in mortgage rates and the psychological impact on consumer confidence would help," he said.
